title: CLOSING BELL: Chalmers must act on super test review
full_text:
There's a lot at stake as deliberations about the future of the nation's superannuation performance test wrap up.
And what's abundantly clear is that Treasurer Jim Chalmers should press ahead with an overhaul of the test. That's because he has an opportunity to make a meaningful and positive change in our financial markets, rather than just trying to bolster investment by superannuation funds in areas such as venture capital, the energy transition or affordable housing.
Chalmers can't afford to sit idle because the overriding issues confronting Australia's capital markets and financial infrastructure are too pressing to ignore. They include the rise in passive and algorithmic investing, a hollowing out of the active funds management industry, the evolution of artificial intelligence, heightened and sometimes extreme volatility in stocks, the increased prevalence of index hugging and the dearth of new ASX listings.
In May, Treasury released a consultation paper to assess a strengthening of the performance test. Now Chalmers is preparing to receive an extensive report from Treasury on the proposed reforms over the next four to six weeks, sources close to the process said on the condition of anonymity. Submissions were received in June and since then, Treasury representatives have been consulting super funds and other stakeholders, while several investment banks and listed companies have also provided views on the best way forward.
Asked about the timeframe for Treasury to report back to Chalmers, a spokeswoman didn't respond by the time of publication. Stakeholders are also yet to see the submissions received by the department, as Treasury is yet to publicly release them.
Much of the criticism about the performance test centres on large superannuation funds being too fearful of risk-taking and therefore gravitating towards mirroring key domestic share indices for fear of failing the test.
Just last year, for example, there were reports some industry funds were trying to make up for their fund managers' underweight positions in banks by buying the stocks directly, leading to upward pressure in bank shares.
And while many fund managers have a vested interest in seeing the performance test overhauled, they also make valid points about its distortions.
Long-only equities house WaveStone Capital, which manages $5.4 billion, used its submission to highlight structural distortions in Australian equity markets that could over time "undermine the long-term member outcomes it is designed to protect".
"A market that allocates capital less efficiently, discovers prices less accurately, and stewards companies less effectively is ultimately worse for every superannuation member," the submission said. "Superannuation clients have increasingly sought 'enhanced index' or 'low-tracking-error active' mandates that constrain portfolio construction in ways that were not present prior to the test's introduction."
The submission also pointed to the extreme volatility plaguing large stocks, in part due to capital clusters and passive funds concentrated at the larger end of the ASX. It cited examples including Cochlear's earnings guidance downgrade in April, which saw the stock suffer a single-session decline of about 40 per cent.
The WaveStone document also identified myriad challenges for ASX initial public offering candidates.
"A market dominated by benchmark-sensitive capital is structurally less able to provide flexible, conviction-driven funding to new listings and smaller companies seeking to access equity markets," it said.
"High-conviction pre-IPO or small-cap allocation creates tracking error against the ASX 300 because such positions are, by definition, outside the benchmark.
"Over time, this risks reducing the dynamism of the listed corporate sector and limiting the pipeline of emerging companies able to access equity markets efficiently."
Paradice Investment Management founder David Paradice is also an advocate for changes to the performance test, noting the market distortions it created around a greater desire for index-hugging had led to a spate of fund managers shutting up shop."People need to focus on net returns ... not what's cheapest. When you go buy a car, you don't necessarily buy the cheapest because it might not be any good," he says.
As well as WaveStone, which is navigating a period of underperformance but has beaten its benchmark over the past 12 years, other fund managers who made submissions to Treasury on the performance test include Quest Asset Partners, ASX-listed Perpetual and Allan Gray.
The performance test was introduced in 2021 following the Productivity Commission's 2018 inquiry into the superannuation sector's efficiency and competitiveness. So a five-year stocktake of the framework underpinning the test and how it has changed behaviour and the shape of the market makes a lot of sense.
The test is administered by the prudential regulator and ranks super funds on yearly and longer-term returns on investments, after fees, against a benchmark created by the agency.
A super fund product fails if it underperforms that benchmark by 50 basis points or more, and products that fail the test in consecutive years are banned from accepting new members.
It hasn't, however, been set and forget by regulators and Treasury. There were tweaks made to the test in 2023, including extending the testing period from eight to 10 years, and that was followed in 2024 by a round of consultation on the merits of the test's design and scope.
The latest performance test review, however, is reasonably targeted. It asks for feedback around four proposed options including adjusting for emerging and alternative asset classes, introducing an assessment of risk-adjusted returns, routinely reviewing the benchmarks being used and expanding the test to cover a greater universe of products.
In the performance test's early years it did work well in that it weeded out perennial underperformers and instilled more accountability in the market around investment decisions, but the unintended consequences have also been notable. And Treasury's latest consultation paper admitted that the number of products failing the test had declined significantly since its 2021 introduction.
It feels as though the perverse outcomes created by the test have been well and truly outweighed by its initial positive results.
Quest's submission pointed to specific distortions the firm believes are linked to the performance test, including that some 30 per cent of all trades happen at 4.10pm each trading day. "That is not a market engaged in price discovery - it is a market organised around index mechanics. The performance test created this," it said.
"Australia's listed equity market is not simply a trading venue. It is economic infrastructure: the primary mechanism by which businesses access long-term growth capital, and by which Australian savers participate in business ownership. Decades of active capital allocation through the ASX have funded the businesses that employ Australians and generate the income that flows into superannuation. Index-hugging does not destroy this infrastructure overnight. But it gradually hollows it out."
Allan Gray's submission goes further, warning Treasury against Band-Aid solutions for the performance test, urging it to start with a blank sheet.
"Failing or passing a performance test can, these days, easily turn on simply owning or not owning one of today's mega-caps (e.g. SpaceX, Nvidia or CBA)," it said.
It's now up to Chalmers to seize the opportunity to overhaul the performance test in a way that promotes the efficiency and resilience of our capital markets.
